analysis.one_liner: Speeds cheaper generic drugs to market by curbing brand-name drug patent delays.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote, despite 21 Senate cosponsors including two Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have tightened the rules brand-name drug companies use to keep cheaper generic copies off the market. Brand companies would have to register their patents with the FDA within 30 days of a drug's approval or lose the right to sue over them. A single patent challenge could no longer automatically freeze a generic's approval for 30 months, and generic companies that sat on their rights or cut side deals would forfeit their head start. The Congressional Budget Office, cited in the bill itself, estimated that wider generic use could save drug purchasers $8 to $10 billion a year, with generics costing 25 to 60 percent less per prescription.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers — especially seniors and the uninsured, who pay for brand-name drugs out of pocket or through premiums — would gain faster access to generics priced 25 to 60 percent below brand names. Generic drug manufacturers would gain faster, more predictable approval timelines and protection of their confidential formulation information during patent disputes.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would save purchasers an estimated $8 to $10 billion a year, with generics costing 25 to 60 percent less than brand-name drugs — an average of $15 to $30 per prescription, per CBO estimates cited in the bill.
Brand companies would have to register patents with the FDA within 30 days of approval or lose the right to sue generic makers for infringement, closing a common delay tactic.
The automatic 30-month freeze on generic approvals would no longer apply to patents issued after a drug's approval, so late-added patents could not be used to repeatedly restart the delay clock.

A generic first-filer that fails to market the drug, withdraws its application, or settles in ways that delay competition would forfeit its 180-day exclusive sales window to the next generic applicant, preventing both sides of the market from staging false standoffs.
The FTC would report to Congress within five years on whether the changes actually brought products to market faster and lowered drug prices.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies, which would lose their most effective tools for extending patent monopolies beyond expiration — automatic 30-month stays, late-filed patent listings, and lightly policed exclusivity standoffs. Patent holders would also face stricter deadlines and limited remedies.

drawbacks.text: Brand companies and patent advocates argued the bill tilted too far against patent holders: it bars lawsuits over unregistered patents, limits the 30-month stay for later-issued patents, and tells courts to disregard a generic maker's ability to pay damages when deciding whether to block sales — remedies that exist to protect inventors' exclusivity while a patent is tested in court.

The new forfeiture rules for the 180-day generic exclusivity period are intricate, with six separate forfeiture triggers and exception carve-outs at the Health Secretary's discretion; badly administered, they could discourage first-filers from taking on patent challenges at all.
The bill does not cap any prices itself; its benefits depend entirely on generic companies winning court challenges and actually bringing products to market, which can still take years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential gains are large and well documented — billions a year in savings for anyone buying prescription drugs. The cost falls on brand-name patent holders, though some of their objections are legitimate: the bill narrows patent remedies in ways that could weaken incentives to develop new drugs, and the forfeiture machinery adds real complexity. On balance, the savings to consumers dwarf the costs, and the bill was a serious attempt to fix known loopholes rather than a blanket override of patents.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Schumer introduced the bill on January 7, 2003, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
Twenty-one senators cosponsored the bill, 19 Democrats and 2 Republicans, including John McCain, Susan Collins, Edward Kennedy, and Hillary Clinton.
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action ever taken; the bill's last recorded action is its referral to committee on January 7, 2003.

The bill's own findings cite FTC concerns about brand and generic companies entering private financial deals that restrain trade and raise drug prices, along with CBO savings estimates of $8 to $10 billion a year.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers, which kept the delay tactics the bill targeted — automatic 30-month stays and late patent listings — for the rest of the Congress, while consumers kept paying brand-name prices where generics were held off.

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.role: U.S. Senator from New York, lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized the Senate's largest bipartisan cosponsor group for a generic drug access bill that session.

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.role: U.S. Senator from Arizona, Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as one of only two Republicans, giving it bipartisan cover.

for.name: 21 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including Sens. Collins, Kennedy, Clinton, Leahy, Daschle, and Durbin.

for.name: Generic drug industry
for.role: Manufacturers of lower-cost copies of brand-name drugs
for.what_they_did: Would benefit directly from faster approvals; the bill's findings echo their long-standing complaints about 30-month stays and pay-for-delay deals.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee (Judd Gregg, R-NH), 108th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee despite its cosponsor count.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Would have lost the automatic 30-month stay, late patent listing tactics, and lightly policed exclusivity standoffs the bill targeted; the bill's own findings cite FTC concerns about brand-generic restraint of trade.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors were senators — 19 Democrats and 2 Republicans (McCain and Collins) — but the bill never advanced past its Democratic-sponsored referral to the HELP committee, whose Republican chair took no action.

industries.note: The bill would remove their main tools for keeping generics off the market after patents expire: the automatic 30-month approval freeze on patent suits, protection for patents filed late, and unregistered patents they could still sue over. Their gain is extended monopoly pricing at consumers' expense.

Faster, more predictable approvals and confidential treatment of their formulation data would expand their market, but the bill also strips their 180-day exclusivity if they stall, withdraw, or settle in ways that delay marketing — closing loopholes on their side too.

industries.industry: Consumers and payers of prescription drugs
industries.note: Seniors, the uninsured, employers, and insurers buying brand-name drugs would benefit from generics arriving sooner; CBO figures cited in the bill put the potential savings at $8-10 billion a year.
